digests.narrative:
The chokepoint got narrower this week, and it was the sellers who narrowed it. Coherent told its call it does not see any time in the near future when it would sell indium phosphide lasers externally. Applied Optoelectronics had already said it cannot participate meaningfully in first-generation co-packaged optics deployments because it has to prioritise lasers for its own transceivers. Two of the largest qualified InP sources are now internal-only, which is disclosure rather than inference, and it leaves buyers of merchant continuous-wave lasers with a shorter list. That is the whole basis of the analyst's Sivers and MACOM positioning — with the caveat, from his own reading, that MACOM has no meaningful capacity coming online until the end of 2027.

Lumentum's print and transcript dated the rest of it. Revenue of $1.01B, up 109% year on year, guidance of $1.225-1.275B at 39.5-40.5% operating margin, its target operating model reached more than a quarter early. But management placed the ultra-high-power laser and CPO ramp in the second half of calendar 2027 and disclosed a first external-light-source module order for delivery in that same window; Coherent said fiscal 2027 is essentially booked out, with long-term agreements running toward the end of the decade and no push-out in CPO demand. So the revenue being reported now is 1.6T datacom optics. Co-packaged optics is a contracted 2027 event. The live pricing datapoint is Lumentum saying it has been surprised at its ability to price up even in CW and expects to hold a premium as Chinese suppliers arrive — both it and AOI describe those suppliers as years behind their stated output.

Below the majors, two small-cap threads were added and should be kept separate from the majors' evidence. Sivers signed a $3.4M development programme with SemiNex for CPO, DFB laser arrays and optical amplifiers, targeting early production in H2 2027 — a development agreement, not volume. POET, where the analyst took a small position, is now a balance-sheet case rather than a demand case: roughly $830M of cash against about a $1.25B market capitalisation, a 12M optical-engine annual capacity target for 2027, and by his own description no visible demand to fill it beyond Lumilens. The desk's standing discipline is unchanged — reported and modelled numbers read alike at speed, and almost everything above the substrate layer is still modelled.
keyPoints: COHR will not sell InP lasers externally 'any time in the near future'; AAOI is absent from first-gen CPO — merchant CW supply narrows

LITE reports pricing power in CW lasers and says Chinese output claims are unverified; AAOI puts those suppliers 2-3 years behind

digests.narrative:
Allocation is now the whole story. DRAM and HBM capacity for 2027 is described as sold out across Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix, NAND is sold out on current annual capacity, and customers are being allocated only 60-70% of the volumes they requested, with Kioxia and SK Hynix finalising the rest by August. The framing in the feed is that 2027 is the most severe point of the shortage.

Sandisk's fiscal fourth quarter turned that industry narrative into a company number: revenue of $8.97bn, adjusted EPS of $39.25, gross margin near 78%, first revenue recognised from the QLC-based Stargate platform, and a fiscal Q1 2027 guide of $10.3-10.8bn with $44-46 of EPS. That is the NAND-specific pricing evidence the desk had been holding out for.

What the theme cannot tell you is where in the cycle this sits. The shares trade at a single-digit multiple of guided earnings, which is the market pricing a peak the guidance does not show. He remains explicitly bullish on memory while noting the sector's attention has rotated to photonics — his own framing of a market that moves from bottleneck to bottleneck.

digests.narrative:
One real datapoint in an otherwise quiet week, and it came from the smallest name in the layer. Tower Semiconductor signed for indium phosphide epiwafers from IQE, and management said the agreement was made to secure the 'strategic III-V epiwafer supply required for that roadmap'. That places a foundry the desk carries here directly inside the optical bottleneck rather than beside it — the first time this layer has produced its own evidence of the shortage instead of reading it off a customer's call.

TSMC appears in the feed only in passing while its own disclosure does the talking: first-half revenue up 35.6% year on year, June alone up 67.9%. The structural point for the whole map is unchanged — the advanced-packaging squeeze is loosening, with industry reporting the CoWoS supply-demand gap narrowing from roughly 20% to 10% by end-2026 and capacity heading toward about 200,000 wafers a month by end-2027. That is why scarcity keeps migrating upstream into lasers, epiwafers and substrates rather than staying in packaging.

GlobalFoundries and Intel are unchanged and unmentioned. The CHIPS silicon-photonics award remains GlobalFoundries' whole case, and Intel's disclosed 14A schedule still puts risk production in 2027 and volume in 2028.

digests.narrative:
Nebius reported, and the shape of the sector's evidence changed. Revenue was $582.3M, up 454% year on year and 46% sequentially, with AI Cloud adjusted EBITDA margin around 50% — a 24% to 45% to 50% progression — against $8.04B of cash. Guidance was reiterated rather than raised: 2026 revenue of $3.0-3.4B and exit ARR of $7-9B. More usefully, the disclosures the desk had been asking for arrived with it: four customer agreements averaging over $1B each, roughly 70% of second-quarter deals carrying prepayments, more than $9B of prepayments expected in 2026 against $40B+ of commitments, contracted power raised again from about 4GW to 5GW, and annual contract value above $40M per megawatt on short-term third-quarter capacity. Management's line was that it could sell its entire 2027 capacity on today's terms.

That closes most of the gap the desk flagged last week: 'sold out' can now be sized. The bear case has not moved — $5.66B of capex and a GAAP net loss, funded ahead of the revenue. IREN is the opposite case and unchanged: the seats found nothing to trade before its 16 September print, with AI Cloud still the minority of a business whose last reported quarter was $144.8M of revenue, $111.2M of it mining. CoreWeave's backlog above $100B remains the cohort's demand anchor, and it belongs to CoreWeave.

Revenue inflections across the cohort still cluster in the second half of 2027, so these names are priced today on contracts and prepayments rather than delivered revenue. Nebius has at least now published the contract terms. The others have not.

digests.narrative:
The indium phosphide substrate case strengthened this week without a substrate company reporting anything. Lumentum told its call it has been surprised at its ability to price up continuous-wave lasers and expects to sustain that premium; Coherent added the matching constraint from the other side, saying it is not short of assembly and test capacity, only of indium phosphide production ramp. Pricing power at the laser layer is what makes prepaid wafer capacity beneath it rational, and AXT already holds reservation deposits of $43.5M from Lumentum and $22.3M from Coherent. AEHR, on the test leg, took another $22M follow-on order for AI processor wafer-level burn-in from its lead customer — a repeat purchase from the same buyer, which is firmer than most of what this layer runs on.

Glass-core substrate becomes visible in this layer for the first time, and the news is a delay. Samsung Electro-Mechanics has pushed the start of glass substrate operations to 2028 from the second half of 2027, citing a bottleneck in customer reliability evaluations of prototypes, and SKC Absolics has moved mass production to the first half of 2027 from the second half of 2026, with final validation targeted by year-end. That is against a Samsung/Dongwoo joint venture earlier flagged as targeting full commercialisation in H2 2027 on KRW 482.1B of planned capital, with LPKF named as the equipment beneficiary via its LIDE and TGV tooling and a claimed 80% penetration among major players. The analyst reads the slippage as a sign the ramp is imminent rather than dead. That is an interpretation; the datapoint itself is negative, and volume at LPKF tracks these dates.

Substrate scarcity is not confined to glass. Samsung Electronics is reported to be struggling to secure large FC-BGA substrates, with Ibiden asking for long-term agreement guarantees and Samsung Electro-Mechanics seeking prepayments — the same prepay-to-secure-supply pattern AXT already shows in indium phosphide. The policy thread is unchanged and slower: direct government investment into scandium, graphite, boron and magnet rare earths continues to treat upstream inputs as strategic rather than commercial, with still no revenue attached at any listed name the desk tracks.

LPK.DE volume tracks those dates — LIDE/TGV tooling, claimed 80% penetration among major players
Samsung reported short of large FC-BGA substrate; Ibiden wants LTA guarantees, SEMCO wants prepayments

digests.narrative:
The layer's read-through hardened in one direction and went quiet in the other. The analyst's survey of this month's optical earnings places Broadcom inside the narrowed Western pool for first-generation co-packaged optics alongside Lumentum, Coherent and Sivers, while MACOM reads as a near-package rather than co-packaged participant and Semtech has shown nothing visible since its HieFo acquisition.

The layer's main claim is still the DSP and TIA bottleneck AOI flagged on its call — the signal-processing and amplifier silicon inside every transceiver — and it is still second-hand. The practical consequence is unchanged: transceiver revenue forecasts built purely on laser capacity understate the constraint chain, because a module needs the DSP and the TIA too.

No company disclosure from the named suppliers themselves, and no dedicated desk position. This remains a layer whose importance to the buildout is obvious and whose evidence is entirely other people's earnings calls.

digests.narrative:
The thinnest theme in the book and the least changed: three posts, all from July, all about Corning, and nothing since. The analyst's position is that Corning's glass bridge has potential per Morgan Stanley but is hard to displace FAU incumbents like FOCI in the short term, and that much of the earnings case rests on 2028 TAM for fibre array units rather than anything shipping now. Co-packaged optics has not scaled up yet, so the uncertainty runs both ways — CPO delay reports hurt the FAU case and the glass bridge case at the same time. Corning fell 11.4% in the July Bloomberg-framing selloff, in line with the rest of the complex rather than for anything specific to it.

One structural note for the desk rather than the analyst: the live glass-substrate news does not appear here. Samsung Electro-Mechanics and SKC Absolics both slipped their glass-core substrate timelines this month, and that thread is filed under materials because it reaches the book through LPKF rather than Corning. Anyone reading this theme for glass substrate progress is reading the wrong card.

Conviction stays low. One ticker, no company disclosure in the feed, and an earnings case dated to 2028.

digests.narrative:
The humanoid trade is now entirely a comparables trade. Unitree's retail subscription came in more than 8,000 times oversubscribed, and derivative markets imply a market capitalisation around $29-30B against an official listing target of $5.7-6.2B later this month — four to five times the offer. The analyst's argument for taking that seriously is that pre-IPO perpetuals have tracked opening prices closely at Cerebras and SpaceX, and that a sector leader tends to lift the valuations of everyone beside it, as Lumentum did across optics.

What none of it supplies is an order book. Agility Robotics still arrives via CCXI at roughly $2.5B pre-money in Q4, backed by SoftBank, NVIDIA, Amazon and Foxconn, with no disclosed humanoid unit economics anywhere in the public comparables. The analyst holds the position and says so plainly; his own framing is halo effect, not fundamentals, and he names Ouster, Harmonic Drive and Leaderdrive as supply-chain exposure rather than as calls.

Aeva's reframing as a CPO and NPO optical source name, linked to the same laser supply chain the photonics book runs on, is unchanged. Robotics remains venture-shaped exposure wearing public tickers, and this week widened the valuation gap without improving the evidence.

digests.narrative:
This week's accelerator-layer evidence came from the box builders rather than the chip designers. Supermicro guided FY2027 revenue to $65-72B against roughly $52.4B of consensus and logged more than $60B of new orders, against a market capitalisation the analyst puts near $20-25B; he took a short-term position on the print and flagged 2027 gross margin as the thing the call had to answer. Read as an accelerator demand signal it is a large one, because those boxes are mostly full of NVIDIA silicon — but it is a server OEM's order book, not a chip vendor's disclosure.

AMD is unchanged from last week. Data-centre revenue was $6.7bn, up 107% year on year, attributed in the 10-Q to EPYC processors and MI350-series parts rather than MI450. Helios entered production with shipments starting at the end of the third quarter, and the first gigawatt of the announced Anthropic deployment begins in the first half of 2027. The co-packaged optics read-through the feed keeps drawing from AMD's rack roadmap to the laser suppliers is therefore a 2027 event at the earliest.

NVIDIA barely features beyond breadth lists and its position is unchanged: management's own guidance is that supply stays constrained through the entire life of Vera Rubin, which is what underwrites the upstream bottleneck thesis. The offsetting fact is concentration — data centre is roughly 92% of revenue, sold to a handful of buyers.

digests.narrative:
The payers keep confirming demand and keep getting punished for funding it. Google Cloud backlog reached $514bn, up more than $50bn sequentially, with just over half expected to convert to revenue inside 24 months and cloud revenue up 82% to $24.8bn. Amazon raised capex to $220bn and said explicitly that even that will not meet 2026 demand, with 2027 the same. Meta narrowed full-year capex upward to $130-145bn. The combined 2026 figure across the four runs to roughly $720-745bn and remains the cleanest demand signal on the map.

Two qualifications belong on it. Part of the raises is memory cost inflation rather than incremental units, so the dollars overstate the pull on optics. And none of these companies disclose accelerator mix or capacity, so every read-through to a named supplier is inference.

The new development is in the private market rather than the public one. Vantage Data Centers, the developer-operator whose anchor tenant is Oracle for Stargate, is exploring a listing at around $100B, and an Anthropic listing is being discussed at a reported $2T valuation — which the analyst says openly he does not believe. Neither is a disclosure about compute demand; both are a statement about how capital markets are pricing access to it. The cash cost at the payers is meanwhile visible: Meta's quarterly free cash flow fell to $784m against $31.1bn of capex, while Alphabet's spend is funded by an accelerating business, which is why it is the desk's accumulate leg here.
keyPoints: Google Cloud backlog $514bn, up more than $50bn sequentially; cloud revenue up 82% to $24.8bn
Amazon capex raised to $220bn, with management saying it still will not meet 2026 demand

digests.narrative:
This layer exists because the desk built it, not because the feed produced it. Every thesis that touches power reaches it through a list rather than an argument. Bloom Energy is the only sustained name: it appears in a late-July recap for 166% year-on-year revenue growth with expanding margins and raised 2026 guidance, and again in the note that grid power bottlenecks triggered a five-fold increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for its fuel cells. That financing line is the clearest power-constraint datapoint anywhere in the feed.

The second thread is a components one and sits mostly outside the US listed set: a shortage of high-power cylindrical cells for battery backup units, with Samsung SDI supplying Simplo, which assembles for Meta and Amazon, and both Panasonic and Samsung reported short. Vertiv, Eaton, EnerSys and BorgWarner are named only as adjacent read-throughs, and the analyst says plainly it is outside his domain.

GE Vernova and Constellation carry no analyst mentions at all, which is exactly the tiering caveat this layer was built to expose: grid interconnection, transformers and on-site generation are load-bearing for every gigawatt in the neocloud and hyperscaler digests, and the feed prices none of it. Conviction is low because the evidence is thin, not because the constraint is.
